title: Post-Course Portfolio: Online Connect Four / Battleship
descriptionMarkdown:
# Online Connect Four / Battleship

## Position in the curriculum
Post-course portfolio expansion: build after the Real-Time Online Tic-Tac-Toe, whose WebSocket connection handling and turn-validation pattern this project extends into a larger board and, for Battleship specifically, a phase where each player has genuinely hidden information the other must never see.

## Beyond what the lessons taught
This project assumes the WebSocket research already done for Tic-Tac-Toe. Pick one game (Connect Four is the simpler choice; Battleship is harder because of the hidden-ship-placement phase) rather than building both.

## Already-proven foundation
Chapter 23's boundary-handling discipline (never send a caller data they are not authorized to see) is the central new requirement here, applied for the first time to game state itself rather than to an HTTP response body: a Battleship player's view of the board must never include the opponent's unrevealed ship positions.

## Project scope
For Connect Four: a 7-wide, 6-tall board, gravity-based column drops, and a win check for four in a row horizontally, vertically, and both diagonals, run efficiently rather than by re-scanning the whole board after every single move. For Battleship: a private ship-placement phase per player (validated server-side: no overlapping ships, no ships extending off the board), followed by alternating shots, where each player's broadcast view of the board shows only hits/misses on the opponent's grid, never the opponent's actual unrevealed ship positions. Whichever game you choose, hold each session's full authoritative state on the server, broadcasting to each connected player only the view they are entitled to see, and reject an out-of-turn or invalid move exactly as in the Tic-Tac-Toe project.

## Required evidence
- A win/game-over detection test suite (four-in-a-row in all four directions for Connect Four, or all-ships-sunk for Battleship).
- For Battleship specifically: a test proving a player's outgoing broadcast never contains the opponent's unrevealed ship-position data, inspected at the JSON/message level, not just "the UI doesn't display it."
- A ship-placement validation test suite (overlapping ships rejected, off-board placement rejected) if you chose Battleship, or a column-full rejection test if you chose Connect Four.
- A concurrency test for two near-simultaneous moves/shots in the same session, confirming turn order is enforced correctly.
- The same disconnect-handling documentation and test as the Tic-Tac-Toe project, adapted to this game.

## Review and completion
A reviewer plays a full game to completion, then — for Battleship specifically — inspects the raw WebSocket messages sent to one player during the game and confirms the other player's ship positions never appeared in any message before being legitimately revealed by a hit.
learningObjectives: Extend a validated turn-based game architecture to a larger board and richer win conditions
Enforce per-player information asymmetry at the server boundary, never relying on the client to hide data
Validate a private setup phase (ship placement) server-side before gameplay begins
Efficiently check a win condition incrementally rather than rescanning the entire board on every move
Inspect raw outgoing messages, not just the UI, to verify a confidentiality requirement actually holds
